extracted.intended_audience: employers, HR professionals, labor and employment attorneys, unions, policy advocates, and other stakeholders affected by FLSA part 541 overtime exemption rules
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for defining and delimiting the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) executive, administrative, professional (EAP) and highly compensated employee (HCE) exemptions under Department of Labor Part 541 regulations, including salary tests, duties tests, special rules, and updating methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnings criteria as a screen for bona fide EAP employment
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount paid to an employee is 'a valuable and easily applied index to the `bona fide' character of the employment for which [the] exemption is claimed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The salary level test helps identify bona fide EAP employees, provides a practical guide for employers and employees, tends to reduce litigation, and ensures nonexempt employees receive overtime protection. Stakeholders have historically supported retaining earnings thresholds for these reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary-basis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the EAP exemption, employees generally must be paid on a salary or fee basis at least the amount specified in the regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salary-basis is a separate element of the exemption distinct from the duties test. Under the HCE test, employees must receive at least the standard salary portion on a salary or fee basis without regard to nondiscretionary bonuses and incentive payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties test (executive, administrative, professional)
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee's job duties must primarily involve executive, administrative, or professional duties as defined by the regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties tests complement the salary/duration criteria and largely determine exemption status for most salaried white-collar employees. The Department retained the standard duties test in prior rules and did not change duties criteria in some recent updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long test (historical two-test system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical 'long' test paired a lower earnings threshold with a more rigorous duties test that generally limited the performance of nonexempt work to no more than 20 percent of an employee's hours worked in a workweek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the long test, lower-paid employees who met the long salary level but not the short salary level were subject to stricter duties analysis to ensure bona fide EAP status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short test (historical two-test system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical 'short' test paired a higher salary level with a less rigorous duties test, with no specified limit on the performance of nonexempt work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees meeting the higher short salary level were considered more likely to meet duties requirements and thus were subject to a short-cut duties test for exemption status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single standard test (post-2004 structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2004 rule eliminated the long/short tests and replaced them with a single standard test that paired a standard salary level with a standard duties test (substantially equivalent to the prior short duties test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting to a single test broadened the exemption by removing the long-test duties protections for some lower-paid employees; setting the standard salary level determines how much that broadening occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard salary level methodology (percentile-based choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department has set salary thresholds using percentile-based methodologies (e.g., 20th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers in the lowest-wage Census Region and/or in retail; 40th percentile in 2016 for the South).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of percentile (and geographic/industry base) materially affects who is exempt. The Department has explained tradeoffs: lower percentiles retain screening for lower-paid workers but risk excluding fewer white-collar workers, while higher percentiles extend overtime protection to more workers but may make many formerly exempt workers nonexempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly Compensated Employee (HCE) test requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCE test pairs a minimal duties requirement—customarily and regularly performing at least one of the exempt duties or responsibilities of an EAP employee—with a high total annual compensation requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HCE thresholds have changed over time (e.g., $100,000 in 2004; $134,004 in 2016; $107,432 in 2019). The HCE test applies only to employees whose primary duty includes performing office or non-manual work. Under HCE rules employees must receive at least the standard salary portion on a salary or fee basis regardless of nondiscretionary bonuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of nondiscretionary bonuses, incentive payments, and commissions to satisfy salary level
rubrics_metrics.description: Nondiscretionary bonuses, incentive payments, and commissions paid on an annual or more frequent basis may be used to satisfy up to 10 percent of the standard or special salary levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2016 rule allowed employers to credit such payments paid at least quarterly toward up to 10 percent of the standard salary; the 2019 rule allowed credit for payments made at least annually. The HCE salary portion requirement is applied without regard to these bonus credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special salary levels for territories and specific industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Special salary levels apply for certain U.S. territories and industries (e.g., Puerto Rico, Guam, U.S. Virgin Islands, CNMI; American Samoa; a special weekly 'base rate' for employees in the motion picture producing industry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territories that became subject to the federal minimum wage lost special higher thresholds historically; Department updates can apply the standard salary level to territories subject to federal minimum wage and maintain/adjust special levels where appropriate (American Samoa, motion picture industry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employees not subject to salary tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain employees—doctors, lawyers, teachers, and outside sales employees—are not subject to salary tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other groups (e.g., academic administrative personnel and computer employees) are subject to special or contingent earning thresholds rather than the general standard salary test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer burden of proof for exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer bears the burden of establishing the applicability of any exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Job titles and job descriptions do not determine exemption status, nor does merely paying an employee a salary rather than an hourly rate. Employers must demonstrate that salary, duties, and any other elements meet regulatory criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular updating mechanism for earnings thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department proposed and is finalizing a mechanism to update the standard salary level and HCE total annual compensation threshold periodically (initially July 1, 2024 and every 3 years thereafter) to reflect current wage data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine updates prevent erosion of the thresholds' effectiveness due to wage growth, reduce unpredictability of large, infrequent increases, and provide stability and certainty to employers and employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal: standard salary level at 35th percentile of lowest-wage Census Region
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM proposed increasing the standard salary level to the 35th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers in the lowest-wage Census Region (the South), equivalent to $1,059 per week based on NPRM data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department's rationale: restore the salary level's screening function, account for the shift to a one-test system, distribute impacts so some lower-salaried employees regain overtime protection without excluding too many white-collar employees based solely on salary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal: increase HCE threshold to 85th percentile nationally
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM proposed raising the HCE test's total annual compensation requirement to the annual equivalent of the 85th percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers nationally (equivalent to $143,988 per year based on NPRM data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department reasoned this would reserve HCE status for employees at the top of today's earnings distribution and avoid inadvertently exempting large numbers of employees in high-wage regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of salary level and duties test (screening function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Salary and duties components complement each other; the salary threshold functions as a screening test while duties determine exemption in most cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples show that switching from two tests to one (or changing the salary threshold) changes how many employees are covered by the duties protections. For instance, under the 2004 single standard test, an employee earning just over the standard salary could be exempt even if they would have failed the long duties test because the long test's stricter duties cap was removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20 percent cap on nonexempt work under historical long duties test
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the long duties test (introduced in 1940/1949 changes), executive and professional employees were limited to performing no more than 20 percent of nonexempt work each workweek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limit was used to ensure that lower-paid salaried employees claiming exemption were, in practice, performing primarily exempt duties; later rule structures removed the explicit 20% cap but the legacy informs current debates about appropriate salary thresholds.
